title: Kona Remote 160 CR Review: Like a Process with Battery Options for Short & Long Rides
content:
If the Kona Process is “the mountain biker’s mountain bike,” then that would make the Remote 160 CR the mountain biker’s ebike? The e-biker’s mountain bike? Whatever you want to call it, just know that if you like the ride of the Kona Process mountain bikes but want a little boost, you should love the new Remote 160 CR.

Built with a carbon frame, 160mm of travel front and rear, and 29″ wheels, the Remote 160 CR starts off pretty close to the Process 153 CR. That’s before you figure in the electric motor, of course. The Remote gets its extra go from a Bosch Performance Line SX motor with 60Nm of max torque and 600W of max motor power. That puts it at the higher end of what most would call the lightweight or SL ebike tier. It still provides noticeable power, but not ‘cut the tires loose while climbing at full speed’ kind of power.

Along with that relatively conservative torque and power number (especially when compared to recent bikes with up to 150Nm/1500W), the Remote gets a relatively small internal battery. This 400Wh battery is a big part of why a complete Remote 160 CR build comes in at 46.56lbs (21.11kg) with aluminum wheels, bars, stem, and meaty tires. Add the 3.29lb (1.49kg) PowerMore range extender, and you get 650Wh for a total weight of 49.85lbs (22.61kg).

The internal battery is not easily removable, but the included Bosch PowerMore 250 range extender is. We’ll get into this more below, but it’s a good thing this is included right off the bat.

Ebike things are controlled through the Bosch Mini Remote on the handlebar, or through the Kiox 400C integrated display, or through the Bosch Flow App on your phone.

The Kiox display has a bright color screen that is easy to see in bright sunlight, and there is actually a big benefit to it – in the event that your ebike has a problem, it will tell you the error code right on the screen and will even give you a QR code to scan to learn how to fix it. I needed to use this feature just once over the entire summer of testing (error code 510002), and it turned out to be as simple as turning off the motor and turning it back on again. Who needs an IT department?

The screen shows a number of other details like ride metrics, wattage of you and the bike, and assist levels. But its position on the top tube makes it hard to concentrate on while riding, so don’t expect to be watching your power output on the screen if you don’t want to power right into a tree. It’s a bit amusing that the Kiox and Bosch Flow app can do almost everything my cycling GPS computers can, but I still found myself mounting a GPS to the handlebar because it puts it out front where it’s easier to see at a glance with the trail whizzing by.

The Mini Remote is just about perfect. It’s easy to adjust to a comfortable position, and toggling up or down to different assist modes is second nature. Holding the lower button will engage walk mode, which is handy during tricky hike-a-bike sections, and if you have lights installed, the upper button can control those. There’s also a charging port built into the Kiox display for lights or computers, but don’t expect to have too much extra juice to spare.

The battery choice and build of the Remote 160 CR puts the bike in a unique position. Many lightweight ebikes are built to be lithe cross-country or trail racers. This is not that bike. Instead, the Remote 160 CR is most at home sending gnarly lines, hitting big jumps, and generally pushing the limits of your tires.

Built with satisfyingly grippy 29 x 2.5″ Schwalbe Radial tires with an Ultra Soft Magic Mary up front and Soft Albert out back, it’s clear that lightweight components came second to trail-worthy confidence. That extends across the build, with everything somewhat overbuilt in the typical Kona fashion. These bikes are built to ride (and probably crash).

That is all to say that battery life is not exceptional. But depending on what you plan to do with the bike, it may be ideal. Since the bike comes with the PowerMore range extender, it’s almost two bikes in one: a lightweight trail shredder built for shorter rides, or a heavier but still sub-50lb bike that can power you through longer trail missions with smart battery management.

With just the internal battery, I’ve been getting around 1.5hr ride times with something like 1,500′ of climbing on eMTB+ mode. For a lot of people, this will be plenty for a few laps after work, hitting up their smaller local trails, or for anyone who doesn’t need to be on a bike for 3 hours to have fun. Realistically, if you don’t need the extra battery range, you can save a lot of weight by not carrying it around on shorter rides.

For those who do want to ride longer, the PowerMore is the obvious option. With it, I’ve been able to extend ride time to 2-2.5hrs, with 2,500′ of climbing on eMTB+ mode. It’s still limited compared to full-power e-bikes with huge batteries, but it makes all but the longest rides I do on a normal basis possible.

The only catch is that the PowerMore takes the place of the only water bottle holder on the bike. Personally, there are plenty of longer rides that I do on a single bottle, so I’d prefer a bigger battery with a bottle cage, but it’s not a huge issue to have to carry a pack.

It’s worth pointing out that Bosch recommends you installing the PowerMore range extender before starting your ride, rather than adding it after your battery is already depleted. That’s due to the way that the Battery Management System balances power draw from the main battery and the PowerMore, with it switching back and forth between the two to discharge them evenly. This “protects the battery cells, minimizes electrical and thermal stress on the individual cell packs, and can help maximize the overall service life of both batteries.”

The PowerMore includes a clever quick-release mount that allows you to swap the range extender for their own bottle cage in an instant. Over time, the rails do get gunked up a bit, so I sprayed a bit of dry lubricant on them, and it seemed to help. When the PowerMore is installed, it uses a short cable to plug into the charging port of the bike. That makes it a little annoying when you need to charge, as you end up having to charge both the bike and the PowerMore separately. You can’t just plug into one place and charge both. But with the Bosch 4A charger, things are topped off quickly, and you can be back riding in a few hours if needed.

Being a Class 1 ebike, the Remote will cut out the assist as you approach 20mph/32kmh. It never has that OMG this thing is crazy kind of power, but it offers enough to easily get up the hill to hit that next jump line again and again.

The Build

In terms of the build, there were definite high spots, and only a few low spots. The Schwalbe Radial tires are certainly a bright spot. I have a similar setup on another full-power e-bike, and I’m left with the same impression – massive amounts of grip (you can hear it!), a casing that is so supple that you’ll likely need more air pressure than you typically run, and no punctures or issues to speak of.

The SRAM Maven Base brakes offer plenty of stopping power, which is exactly what you need on a bike like this. If I had my choice, it would be the new Maven B1s over the Base model for their slightly more progressive feel, but that’s splitting hairs.

Kona put a lot of thought behind each component in the spec, which is evident in their choice of dropper post lever. While the dropper itself is a TranzX model, the dropper lever is from SRAM. It was chosen because it offered excellent integration with the Maven MMX brake lever mount, and quite a bit of adjustment. I find that the ergonomics are acceptable, though not my favorite, and it also feels like it takes more effort to push than levers that run on cartridge bearings, like the Wolf Tooth ReMote Pro. However, it needs a very short push to activate the dropper, and it’s a better lever than you’ll find on most stock bikes.

The grips are fine, but I would prefer something with a little more cushion, especially with a very stiff 35mm aluminum handlebar beating up your hands.

The suspension duo with a RockShox Super Deluxe Ultimate 230×60 rear shock and a Lyrik Ultimate 160 fork does a lot to tame the trail. It took a while to dial in the settings, and I feel that the compression damping circuit in the fork may be a bit aggressive for my weight, but overall it performed quite well. Note that the bike does not include the integrated fender for the fork – I would buy one of these and install it immediately.

Spare Power

For drivetrain, you get a Shimano Deore Di2 1×11 system that’s powered directly by the ebike battery. The plus side of that wire connecting the derailleur is that you never have to worry about charging the battery for your drivetrain separately.

But what happens when you completely deplete the battery? Are you no longer able to shift or use your lights? Fortunately, the bike has a ‘Light Reserve Mode’ which keeps enough charge to allow you to shift and use your lights to get back to the trail head. This wasn’t set up on my early review sample, so I can’t speak to how it works but Kona assures me that all production bikes will have this setting.

Manual, Manual+, or Automatic Shifting

That connection of the derailleur to the motor also means you also get the eShift capabilities with either full Manual, Manual+, or Full Automatic shifting. Everything should be set up for this when you get your bike, but it’s a good idea to make sure both the bike and rear derailleur are updated first. After that, to access the different shift modes you press the small button on the top of the Shimano shifter.

You’ll see either an ‘M’, ‘M+’, or ‘A’ on the Kiox display for Manual, Manual+, and Automatic shifting modes. Manual works just as you’d expect with you controlling the only shifts. Manual+ makes it so only you can shift when you’re pedaling, but when you coast, the bike will shift into what it thinks will be the proper gear to start pedaling again based on your speed.

And full auto mode relies on a set cadence that you program either through the Kiox display or the Bosch Flow app. It will then shift automatically to keep it in that cadence range.

I used predominantly Manual shifting, but the other modes were fun to mess around with. Manual+ or Automatic could be very useful if you’re a new rider and focusing on just staying on your bike rather than when to shift. For advanced riders though, the ability of a human to know what’s coming on the trail and what gear they should be in before they get there is still superior to a reactionary machine… for now.

Elsewhere in the drivetrain, stubby little 155mm Prowheel carbon cranks are bolted to the motor along with a 34t ring from e13. Those propel a Shimano CUES LG500 chain, which drives a Shimano 11-50t 11-speed cassette. It’s all high-quality stuff that should last quite a while – and even better, it won’t cost a fortune to replace when you inevitably wear it out.

All stock bikes except the small come with 29/29″ wheels, where the small comes as an MX 29/27.5″ build. However, any frame can be built up with an MX wheelset thanks to the flip chip at the rear axle.

The stock wheels are decent, with WTB ST Tough i30 rims laced to Formula hubs in Boost spacing with an HG freehub. That freehub is fine, though it doesn’t have the quickest engagement. On the other end, the freehub on the motor seems to be rather loud and rattle-y when you’re coasting down the trail without any pressure on the pedals. This stands out because otherwise, this is a pretty quiet bike. The motor isn’t the most silent option, but its whines are fairly quiet and inoffensive.

Spread out on the frame, you’ll find smart details that hint toward how this bike is meant to be used. A custom OneUp chain guide is there to keep the chain in place when things get rough. There is a burly chainstay protector along with a skid plate for the motor and a shuttle guard on the downtube to protect against tailgate pad rub. You’ll also find a little mini fender to keep crud out of the main pivot, and a custom charging port with a swinging door to allow for easy use of the PowerMore. That last one doesn’t sound like much, but compared to flimsy rubber plugs on some other bikes, this is a very nice touch.

Retail & Detail

Offered in small, medium, large, and extra-large frames, the Remote 160 CR retails for $7,799. Not cheap, but considering everything you’re getting, it seems like a reasonable price – about $2,500 more than a Process 153 CR.

Riding Away

Riding the Remote 160 CR was enjoyable from the beginning, but it wasn’t until I took this bike to a local jump line that I had that lightbulb moment where I realized what this bike was really intended for. Along those lines, I was very happy to find that this bike didn’t suffer from the power cuts on hard g-outs that older Bosch ebikes experienced. You can pump, drop, and jib to your heart’s content and the motor will continue to propel you forward.

Without the PowerMore, the lighter-weight bike is more fun to throw around and jumps really well. This is the bike for people who complain about longer-travel e-bikes not being poppy and playful enough. The motor is there to help you get up the hill without leaving you gassed for the jumps on the way down. And it’s employed in a way that disappears when you want this to ride like a mountain bike, and not an ebike. As a result, this thing is a serious confidence booster on jumps you would normally shy away from.

On the flip side, if you want your ebike to ride like a worn-out sofa, enveloping everything in its path with never-ending softness, then this probably isn’t the bike for you. Even with the PowerMore installed, the Remote 160 CR still feels more like a Process than a heavy ebike. You can tell that this was a bike built by a team that lives and rides in the Pacific Northwest – in a very good way.

If you’re looking for a bike with the biggest battery and longest range, look elsewhere. But if you want a fun, lightweight bike that’s versatile enough for jump lines on the weekdays and bigger rides on the weekend, you might want to pick up the Remote.

author: Zach Overholt
